sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
In recent years, the increasing frequency and intensity of extreme natural
disasters—such as typhoons, floods, and severe winter storms—driven by global climate
change have posed unprecedented challenges to the secure operation of power systems,
particularly distribution networks. As the “last mile” of electricity delivery, distribution
systems feature geographically dispersed infrastructure and complex network structures
Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 5054 https://doi.org/10.3390/app16105054
Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 5054 2 of 29
yet often exhibit relatively limited resilience against extreme events. Consequently, they are
highly vulnerable to large-scale outages during severe disasters, which can lead to substan-
tial socio-economic losses. Against this backdrop, enhancing the restoration capability of
distribution networks has emerged as a critical research priority in modern power system
studies [1]. System resilience extends beyond the ability to withstand disruptive events; it
also encompasses the capacity to rapidly restore electricity supply following disturbances.
Therefore, restoration capability has become a fundamental metric for evaluating the overall
performance of distribution networks in responding to extreme events [2].
Throughout the lifecycle of a typhoon—from formation and propagation to landfall
and eventual dissipation—the storm’s trajectory, wind-field structure, and intensity exhibit
pronounced temporal dynamics and spatial heterogeneity [3]. Consequently, distribution
network components located at different nodes and lines are subjected to significantly
different wind speed loads at different time periods [4]. Existing studies have attempted
to characterize typhoon wind fields using various modeling approaches. For instance,
Batts-based formulations have been employed to construct static wind-field representa-
tions, where the storm center location and track parameters are used to describe sinusoidal
movement trajectories [5]. An improved wind-field model derived from the Holland for-
mulation was proposed in [6], in which the affected region at a given time is approximated
by two concentric circles. In [7], the post-landfall wind-field evolution is described using
parameters such as landfall angle, pressure difference, and temporal progression. Mean-
while, in [8], directly partitions typhoon-affected regions according to landfall trajectory,
landfall radius, and duration, combined with wind speed variations. Despite these efforts,
most existing studies assume that key wind-field parameters remain constant within the
analyzed time horizon—particularly after landfall—making it difficult to capture critical
dynamic characteristics such as wind-field expansion, intensity attenuation, and trajectory
perturbations during typhoon evolution. Furthermore, with respect to wind-speed correc-
tion, most studies rely primarily on surface roughness coefficients or empirical correction
factors [9], without systematically incorporating the influence of urban morphological fea-
tures, such as building height and building density, on near-surface wind fields. As a result,
the wind-speed estimation at distribution network nodes often remains overly simplified.
Overall, current typhoon modeling approaches still exhibit limitations in representing
spatiotemporal evolution processes, capturing urban environmental effects, and coupling
with the actual geographic information of distribution network infrastructure. Therefore, it
is necessary to develop an integrated typhoon spatiotemporal model that combines static
wind-field representation, dynamic evolution mechanisms, and trajectory-based mobility
characteristics [10], thereby providing a more realistic hazard input for subsequent failure
probability modeling of distribution network components. In summary, existing typhoon
models still lack an integrated framework that simultaneously captures spatiotemporal
evolution processes, urban canopy effects, and coupling with actual distribution network
geographic information, making it difficult to provide sufficiently accurate hazard input
for subsequent component-level failure probability modeling.
Under typhoon conditions, failures in distribution network infrastructure fundamen-
tally originate from the structural impacts of strong wind loads on critical components such
as conductors and utility poles [11]. Existing studies on equipment failures in distribution
systems during typhoon events generally take wind speed as the primary driving factor,
establishing probabilistic mappings between wind speed and the failure likelihood of
conductors or poles to quantify equipment outage risks [12]. For example, the failure prob-
ability of distribution lines has been estimated by comparing calculated conductor wind
loads with their maximum wind-bearing capacity [13]. In [14], the distribution network
is discretized into spatial grids, within which conductors are assumed to share identical
https://doi.org/10.3390/app16105054
Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 5054 3 of 29
failure probabilities, thereby constructing a one-to-one mapping between wind speed and
conductor failure probability. Similarly, ref. [ 15] develops a failure rate calculation and
correction model for utility poles to represent the outage risk of distribution infrastructure
under disaster conditions. Although these studies recognize conductors and poles as the
primary vulnerable components, they typically approximate the failure probability of an
entire distribution line using a single component-level probability. Such simplifications
overlook the structural fact that distribution lines are composed of conductors and poles
connected in series, where the failure of any component may lead to line outages. Moreover,
the modeling of failure mechanisms for conductors and poles remains relatively simplified
in existing work. For instance, when calculating wind loads on conductors, the influence of
the angle between wind direction and conductor orientation is often neglected [16]. Like-
wise, in pole stress assessments, a uniform wind speed parameter is frequently adopted
without considering variations in equivalent wind speed caused by structural characteris-
tics such as pole height, resulting in an insufficiently detailed representation of equipment
vulnerability [17]. After estimating the failure probabilities of individual distribution lines,
most studies directly treat them as the final outage probabilities [18] for network-level anal-
ysis, implicitly assuming independence among different lines. However, under extreme
weather conditions such as typhoons, the dense spatial distribution of poles and the close
proximity of distribution lines mean that the failure of local infrastructure can significantly
increase the damage risk of neighboring components. As a result, failures in distribution
networks often exhibit pronounced spatial correlation and cascading characteristics [19].
Neglecting such network-level dependencies may lead to an underestimation of failure
scales in locally high-risk regions, thereby affecting the accurate assessment of overall
disaster impacts on distribution systems.
Significant progress has been made in recent years in leveraging distributed energy
resources for post-disaster restoration of distribution systems. Existing studies primarily
focus on post-event recovery strategies, including network reconfiguration [20], islanding
operation [21], and the coordinated dispatch of distributed generation and energy storage
resources [22], which can improve load restoration performance to a certain extent. For
instance, ref. [23] establishes a post-disaster restoration framework by optimizing the sit-
ing and capacity allocation of distributed generation units within distribution networks.
Similarly, ref. [24] proposes a restoration strategy that dynamically integrates island parti-
tioning with the spatiotemporal scheduling of emergency power supply vehicles. While
these studies provide valuable ins

sections.title: 2.1 Static Wind Field Model
sections.text:
Existing studies on typhoon modeling indicate that the characterization of typhoon
wind fields can be interpreted as the combined effect of three key components: a static
https://doi.org/10.3390/app16105054
Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 5054 5 of 29
wind-field structure, wind-field evolution dynamics, and the storm trajectory. With respect
to the static wind field, an improved Holland wind-field model is adopted in this study.
Previous research suggests that the spatial influence of a typhoon can be approximately
represented by two concentric circular regions. Within the affected area, the wind speed v
at any location is expressed as a piecewise function of the distance d between that location
and the typhoon eye. Outside the typhoon influence region, the wind speed is assumed
to be zero. For locations within the affected region, the wind speed exhibits a distinct
radial distribution pattern: as the distance d increases from the typhoon eye to the radius
of maximum wind speed, the wind speed increases monotonically; subsequently, as d
increases from the radius of maximum wind speed to the outer radius of typhoon influence,
the wind speed decreases monotonically.

sections.title: 2.2 Dynamic Evolution Model
sections.text:
After a typhoon makes landfall from the ocean into urban areas, its wind speed is
influenced by urban environmental factors such as building height and surface roughness.
As a result, the radii of both the inner and outer wind fields expand according to a certain
proportional coefficient, while the storm intensity gradually weakens. To achieve a more
accurate representation of typhoon evolution after landfall, the landfall time and the
wind-field radius are selected as key input features of the dynamic wind-field evolution
https://doi.org/10.3390/app16105054
Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 5054 6 of 29

central maximum wind speed at the time of landfall, and τd is the intensity decay time
constant, reflecting the decay rate of the typhoon central pressure difference, whose value
is determined from historical data or meteorological forecasts. Solving Equations (3) and
the supplementary equations below simultaneously jointly yields the wind field intensity
and extent within the typhoon-affected region at any given time.
Under strong wind conditions, it is difficult to directly measure the actual wind speed
acting on each component within the geographic environment of a distribution network.
Moreover, wind speed data obtained from nearby meteorological stations cannot accurately
reflect the local wind conditions at specific network nodes. Therefore, it is necessary to
apply wind speed corrections to estimate the actual wind speed at each node. According to
meteorological studies, the wind speed at a given location is closely related to factors such
as relative elevation and surface roughness. In addition, when a typhoon makes landfall
and passes through urban areas, the wind speed may vary significantly due to the influence
of buildings with different heights, which alter the near-surface wind field.

sections.title: 2.3 Path Movement Model
sections.text:
The dynamic typhoon wind field is used to describe the evolution of the wind field
after typhoon landfall, which can be modeled as a series of static wind fields. For the

characterization of the typhoon trajectory, existing studies indicate that the overall path
typically exhibits an S-shaped smooth turning pattern, superimposed with small periodic
sinusoidal oscillations. Accordingly, the specific trajectory function of the typhoon can be
expressed as follows. 

initial phase (rad).

sections.title: 3.1 Distribution Network Framework Fault Scenario Simulation
sections.text:
During typhoon conditions, the conductors and pylons of urban distribution networks
are highly susceptible to typhoon damage. Damage to pylons can cause faults between
node circuits, subsequently leading to outages in the load areas served by those circuits.

sections.title: 2 Line Component Load Effect
sections.text:
Under typhoon conditions, the loads acting on conductors mainly include horizontal
wind loads and gravitational loads. The loads acting on poles and towers primarily consist

poles/towers, they induce cross-sectional stress in the conductors and bending moments in
the pole or tower sections, which are collectively referred to as load effects.

Network Structures

sections.title: 3.2.2 Modeling Photovoltaic Power Output Under Extreme Weather Conditions
sections.text:
Under typhoon conditions, photovoltaic output is significantly affected by extreme
meteorological factors such as strong winds, heavy rainfall, and rapid cloud cover changes,
resulting in substantial deviations between actual output and forecast values. To accurately
characterize photovoltaic output uncertainty during such extreme weather, this paper
introduces a box-type uncertainty set U to describe its fluctuation range, based on the
predicted photovoltaic output PPV∗

the uncertainty radius of PV output. Under typhoon conditions, actual output is typically
lower than the forecast value; statistics show that sudden irradiance reduction can cause
output drops of 30–70%. In the base case, τ = 0.5 is adopted.

sections.title: 4 Multi-Dimensional Collaborative Scheduling Recovery Strategy
sections.text:
In the pre-disaster prevention phase, this study pre-plans the deployment locations
and quantities of mobile energy storage systems. This accounts for extreme photovoltaic
output scenarios and the potential for network reconfiguration, operating under conditions
where both the timing and duration of disasters remain uncertain. The aim is to ensure rapid
emergency response deployment post-disaster, supporting the load restoration process.
Wind turbines are also considered to be recovery resources. Upon transitioning to the
post-disaster recovery phase, a multi-source coordinated restoration optimization model is
established. This model centrally coordinates the dispatch of distributed resources such as
mobile energy storage and electric vehicles, achieving optimized power allocation across
both temporal and spatial dimensions. Consequently, critical load supply is restored to the
greatest extent possible, thereby enhancing the resilience of the distribution network. The
flowchart for the specific modeling and solution process is shown in Figure 2.

sections.text:

reactive power, and power factor, with photovoltaic and wind turbine systems operating
